questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=-\frac{1}{2},{u}_{33}=3,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=-\frac{3}{2}.$

$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & -3 & 5\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & -3 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(\frac{3}{2}){R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =U.\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=-\frac{3}{2},{u}_{33}=-1,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=\frac{3}{2}.$

questions.problem:
Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 8 \\ 5 & 10 & 9\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then ${l}_{31}\cdot {u}_{33}=$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 8 \\ 5 & 10 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-5){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -5 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -5 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{31}=5,{u}_{33}=-6,$ and ${l}_{31}\cdot {u}_{33}=-30.$

questions.problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $C$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}
$$

Given that $C$ has the LU factorization $C=LU,$ then $L=$
questions.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot C=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}C=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}C & =U \\ {E}_{1}C & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ C & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ C & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $H$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}.
$$

Given that $H$ has the LU factorization $H=LU,$ then $L=$
questions.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $H$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1}.
$$

Given that $H$ has the LU factorization $H=LU,$ then $L=$
questions.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+1\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $H$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-8{R}_{1}.
$$

Given that $H$ has the LU factorization $H=LU,$ then $L=$
questions.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-8)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $C$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}
$$

Given that $C$ has the LU factorization $C=LU,$ then $L=$
questions.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot C=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}C=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}C & =U \\ {E}_{1}C & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ C & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ C & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that
$M=[\begin{aligned}5 & 10 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $M=LU,$ then $L=$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $M$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $M$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 10 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{5}){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot M \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}5 & 10 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(\frac{3}{2}){R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot M \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}5 & 10 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}M=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}M & =U \\ {E}_{1}M & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ M & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ M & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ M & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ M & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}5 & 10 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-0.5){R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -0.5 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =U.\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -0.5 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=0.5,{u}_{33}=1,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=0.5.$

questions.problem:
Given that 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -4 \\ 3 & -5 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -4 \\ 3 & -5 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=-\frac{1}{2},{u}_{33}=-2,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=1.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the LU Factorization Using a Single Elementary Row Operation

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Lower Triangular Matrix Given the Elementary Row Operations
canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that a $3 \times 3$ matrix $F$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
R_2:=R_2+R_1, \qquad
	R_3:=R_3+2R_1
$$

Given that $F$ has the LU factorization $F=LU,$ then $L=$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Applying $R_2:=R_2 + {\color{red}1} \cdot R_1$ and then $R_3:=R_3+ {\color{red}2} \cdot R_1$ is equivalent to multiplying $F$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/a99ebe6a4021d9124320439383f1e5351f134a321a353c2dafaa7bbf8555aae7.svg)

Now, since $E_2E_1F=U,$ we can invert $E_2$ and $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}F & =U \\ {E}_{1}F & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ F & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ F & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ F & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ F & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Finding the LU Factorization Using Two or More Elementary Row Operations
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/c21c2b99cdd8480ab891a23f92687d29230da7da9de9bd75a903919e54c48a1f.svg)
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & -6 \\ 0 & -4 & 16\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{5}{4}){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{5}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & -4 & 16\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_2E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_2$ and $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{5}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{5}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{5}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the LU Factorization Using Two or More Elementary Row Operations

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Recall that LU factorization involves writing a matrix $A$ as a product of two matrices $L$ and $U,$ where

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/2e6c0b6fdaf90e3a3e23ed91ffe09cb360bb39325b9a630f1b7219b3188a25db.svg) is a *unit lower triangular matrix* (a lower triangular matrix that has only $1$'s on the main diagonal), and

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/0c5d7337e47a53dfa5bdce8c6f4a96bb1e52ef6054349011a6cc38f29701cc61.svg) is an *upper triangular matrix*.

For example, suppose we're given the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/22dba4fe66ac5478f5d81a68342a01809a360de8e722e809998655e7740bafe8.svg) To perform LU factorization, we need to write $A$ as 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/d4c92b2e8252619f9a1511d166be884b9a2bdb4311eea8e408e8fe75eed6f36c.svg)

As usual, to find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we can reduce the matrix $A$ to *echelon form* while simultaneously performing the same elementary row operations on the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ -2 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} & ⇔ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]=U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

**Caution:** In order to get a unit lower triangular matrix at the end, we have the following restriction while reducing a matrix $A$ to its *echelon form*:

- we can only add multiples of higher rows to lower rows ($R_j:=R_j+k R_i$ where $i < j$), and

- the other elementary row operations (swapping or multiplying a row by a number) are not allowed.

tutorials.content:
Recall that LU factorization involves writing a matrix $A$ as a product of two matrices $L$ and $U,$ where

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/2e6c0b6fdaf90e3a3e23ed91ffe09cb360bb39325b9a630f1b7219b3188a25db.svg) is a *unit lower triangular matrix* (a lower triangular matrix that has only $1$'s on the main diagonal), and

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/0c5d7337e47a53dfa5bdce8c6f4a96bb1e52ef6054349011a6cc38f29701cc61.svg) is an *upper triangular matrix*.

For example, suppose we're given the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/22dba4fe66ac5478f5d81a68342a01809a360de8e722e809998655e7740bafe8.svg) To perform LU factorization, we need to write $A$ as 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/d4c92b2e8252619f9a1511d166be884b9a2bdb4311eea8e408e8fe75eed6f36c.svg)

As usual, to find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we can reduce the matrix $A$ to *echelon form* while simultaneously performing the same elementary row operations on the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ -2 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} & ⇔ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]=U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

**Caution:** In order to get a unit lower triangular matrix at the end, we have the following restriction while reducing a matrix $A$ to its *echelon form*:

- we can only add multiples of higher rows to lower rows ($R_j:=R_j+k R_i$ where $i < j$), and

- the other elementary row operations (swapping or multiplying a row by a number) are not allowed.

Recall that LU factorization involves writing a matrix $A$ as a product of two matrices $L$ and $U,$ where

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/11449bb149f47e379346c7e3fcc2cad78a92d5a17bd3ddbb3a2f53c759d92ec7.svg) is a *unit lower triangular matrix* (a lower triangular matrix that has only $1$'s on the main diagonal), and

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/31fe53feaff3f0643a84d71ae0f1115923f59ca4eba5e894afb1c68c53c548bd.svg) is an *upper triangular matrix*.

For example, suppose we're given the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/9b341d6b06da7f747d451c5d704dbdab8db8e8c8b4e0b0a8c7b5a4fda60132ef.svg) To perform LU factorization, we need to write $A$ as 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14238673/assets/c424d7091f0732e9c9ca68f217c35a9ff6517b80ea8ac094e1ebd85b959106eb.svg)

As usual, to find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we can reduce the matrix $A$ to *echelon form* while simultaneously performing the same elementary row operations on the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ -2 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} & ⇔ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]=U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

**Caution:** In order to get a unit lower triangular matrix at the end, we have the following restriction while reducing a matrix $A$ to its *echelon form*:

- we can only add multiples of higher rows to lower rows ($R_j:=R_j+k R_i$ where $i < j$), and

- the other elementary row operations (swapping or multiplying a row by a number) are not allowed.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the LU Factorization Using a Single Elementary Row Operation
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=-\frac{1}{2},{u}_{33}=3,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=-\frac{3}{2}.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given that A=[3100240−11] has the LU decomposition A=LU, then l32⋅u33=

a
−3
b
12
c
−12
d
−32
e
32
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

A=[3100240−11]R3:=R3+12R2⟺[1000100121]⏞E1⋅A∼[310024003]=U

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix U. Now, since E1A=U, we can invert E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E1A=UA=E1−1UA=[1000100121]−1UA=[1000100−121]⏟L[310024003]⏟U

Therefore, l32=−12,u33=3, and l32⋅u33=−32.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the LU Factorization Using a Single Elementary Row Operation
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 6 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U.\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=-\frac{3}{2},{u}_{33}=-1,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=\frac{3}{2}.$

To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 & 0 \\ 4 & 9 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Lower Triangular Matrix Given the Elementary Row Operations
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot C=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}C=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}C & =U \\ {E}_{1}C & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ C & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ C & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Lower Triangular Matrix Given the Elementary Row Operations
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Lower Triangular Matrix Given the Elementary Row Operations
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+1\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-8)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Applying R2:=R2+2⋅R1 and then R3:=R3+(−8)⋅R1 is equivalent to multiplying H from the left by the following elementary matrices:

[100010−801]⏟E2⋅[100210001]⏟E1⋅H=U

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Lower Triangular Matrix Given the Elementary Row Operations
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot C=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}C=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}C & =U \\ {E}_{1}C & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ C & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ C & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}C=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Lower Triangular Matrix Given the Elementary Row Operations
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & -6 \\ 0 & -4 & 16\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{5}{4}){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{5}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & -4 & 16\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_2E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_2$ and $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{5}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{5}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{5}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 11
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the LU Factorization Using Two or More Elementary Row Operations
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the LU Factorization Using Two or More Elementary Row Operations
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $M$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $M$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 10 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{5}){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot M \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}5 & 10 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(\frac{3}{2}){R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot M \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}5 & 10 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}M=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}M & =U \\ {E}_{1}M & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ M & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ M & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ M & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ M & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{5} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}5 & 10 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that M=[510010−203−3] has the LU decomposition M=LU, then L=

a
[100−15100321]

[10015100−121]

[10015100321]

Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 15
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the LU Factorization Using Two or More Elementary Row Operations
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -4 \\ 3 & -5 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=-\frac{1}{2},{u}_{33}=-2,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=1.$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=$
question.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=-\frac{1}{2},{u}_{33}=3,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=-\frac{3}{2}.$

Given that A=[3100240−11] has the LU decomposition A=LU, then l32⋅u33=

a
−3
b
12
c
−12
d
−32
e
32
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

A=[3100240−11]R3:=R3+12R2⟺[1000100121]⏞E1⋅A∼[310024003]=U

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix U. Now, since E1A=U, we can invert E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E1A=UA=E1−1UA=[1000100121]−1UA=[1000100−121]⏟L[310024003]⏟U

Therefore, l32=−12,u33=3, and l32⋅u33=−32.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem:
Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=$
feedback.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=-\frac{1}{2},{u}_{33}=3,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=-\frac{3}{2}.$

EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

A=[−238012069]R3:=R3+(−6)R2⟺[1000100−61]⏞E1⋅A∼[−23801200−3]=U.

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix U. Now, since E1A=U, we can invert E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization

E1A=UA=E1−1UA=[1000100−61]−1UA=[100010061]⏟L[−23801200−3]⏟U.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the LU Factorization Using a Single Elementary Row Operation
last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 6 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U.\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

A=[−238012069]R3:=R3+(−6)R2⟺[1000100−61]⏞E1⋅A∼[−23801200−3]=U.

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix U. Now, since E1A=U, we can invert E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization

E1A=UA=E1−1UA=[1000100−61]−1UA=[100010061]⏟L[−23801200−3]⏟U.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the LU Factorization Using a Single Elementary Row Operation

solution.reasoning: The operation R_3:=R_3-6R_2 produces upper-triangular U with third row (0,0,-3). Thus L is the identity with l_{32}=6, which reverses that elimination and gives A=LU. This is option b. The provided example supports the method but supplies no answer-key evidence for this question.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 6 & 9\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
feedback.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 6 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U.\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & -3 & 5\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=$
question.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & -3 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(\frac{3}{2}){R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =U.\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=-\frac{3}{2},{u}_{33}=-1,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=\frac{3}{2}.$

last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & -3 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(\frac{3}{2}){R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =U.\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & -7 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=-\frac{3}{2},{u}_{33}=-1,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=\frac{3}{2}.$

?

Given that A=[1230185109] has the LU decomposition A=LU, then l31⋅u33=

a
−36
b
−28
c
32
d
34
e
−30
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

A=[1230185109]R3:=R3+(−5)R1⟺[100010−501]⏞E1⋅A∼[12301800−6]=U

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix U. Now, since E1A=U, we can invert E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E1A=UA=E1−1UA=[100010−501]−1UA=[100010501]⏟L[12301800−6]⏟U

Therefore, l31=5,u33=−6, and l31⋅u33=−30.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the LU Factorization Using a Single Elementary Row Operation
last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 8 \\ 5 & 10 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-5){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -5 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -5 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{31}=5,{u}_{33}=-6,$ and ${l}_{31}\cdot {u}_{33}=-30.$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Given that A=[47049100−5] has the LU decomposition A=LU, then L=

a
[1000100−11]
b
[100110001]
c
[100−110001]
d
[100110−101]
e
[100110011]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

A=[47049100−5]R2:=R2+(−1)R1⟺[100−110001]⏞E1⋅A∼[47002100−5]=U

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix U. Now, since E1A=U, we can invert E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E1A=UA=E1−1UA=[100−110001]−1UA=[100110001]⏟L[47002100−5]⏟U.

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the LU Factorization Using a Single Elementary Row Operation
last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 & 0 \\ 4 & 9 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Given that A=[47049100−5] has the LU decomposition A=LU, then L=

a
[1000100−11]
b
[100110001]
c
[100−110001]
d
[100110−101]
e
[100110011]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

A=[47049100−5]R2:=R2+(−1)R1⟺[100−110001]⏞E1⋅A∼[47002100−5]=U

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix U. Now, since E1A=U, we can invert E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E1A=UA=E1−1UA=[100−110001]−1UA=[100110001]⏟L[47002100−5]⏟U.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the LU Factorization Using a Single Elementary Row Operation

solution.reasoning: Elimination R_2:=R_2-R_1 gives U with rows (4,7,0), (0,2,1), and (0,0,-5). Reversing this operation gives unit-diagonal L with l_{21}=1 and all other off-diagonal entries zero, matching option b. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes the current question's key.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
Given that 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 & 0 \\ 4 & 9 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
feedback.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 & 0 \\ 4 & 9 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

A=[47049100−5]R2:=R2+(−1)R1⟺[100−110001]⏞E1⋅A∼[47002100−5]=U

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix U. Now, since E1A=U, we can invert E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $C$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}
$$

Given that $C$ has the LU factorization $C=LU,$ then $L=$
question.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot C=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}C=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}C & =U \\ {E}_{1}C & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ C & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ C & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}

Question 6
?

Suppose that a 3×3 matrix C is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear: R2:=R2−3R1,R3:=R3+3R1 Given that C has the LU factorization C=LU, then L=

a
[100010−331]
b
[100310−301]
c
[100−310301]
d
[1000103−31]
e
[100310301]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying R2:=R2+(−3)⋅R1 and then R3:=R3+3⋅R1 is equivalent to multiplying C from the left by the following elementary matrices:

[100010301]⏟E2⋅[100−310001]⏟E1⋅C=U

Now, since E2E1C=U, we can invert E2 and E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E2E1C=UE1C=E2−1UC=E1−1E2−1UC=[100−310001]−1[100010301]−1UC=([100310001][100010−301])UC=[100310−301]⏟L⋅U

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Lower Triangular Matrix Given the Elementary Row Operations
last_observation.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot C=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}C=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}C & =U \\ {E}_{1}C & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ C & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ C & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Applying R2:=R2+(−3)⋅R1 and then R3:=R3+3⋅R1 is equivalent to multiplying C from the left by the following elementary matrices:

[100010301]⏟E2⋅[100−310001]⏟E1⋅C=U

Now, since E2E1C=U, we can invert E2 and E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

feedback.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot C=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}C=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}C & =U \\ {E}_{1}C & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ C & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ C & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 7
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Lower Triangular Matrix Given the Elementary Row Operations
last_observation.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $H$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}.
$$

Given that $H$ has the LU factorization $H=LU,$ then $L=$
feedback.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $H$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1}.
$$

Given that $H$ has the LU factorization $H=LU,$ then $L=$
question.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+1\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Suppose that a 3×3 matrix H is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear: R2:=R2+R1,R3:=R3−2R1. Given that H has the LU factorization H=LU, then L=

a
[100110−201]
b
[100−110201]
c
[1000102−11]
d
[1002100−11]
e
[100210−101]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying R2:=R2+1⋅R1 and then R3:=R3+(−2)⋅R1 is equivalent to multiplying H from the left by the following elementary matrices:

[100010−201]⏟E2⋅[100110001]⏟E1⋅H=U

Now, since E2E1H=U, we can invert E2 and E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E2E1H=UE1H=E2−1UH=E1−1E2−1UH=[100110001]−1[100010−201]−1UH=([100−110001][100010201])UH=[100−110201]⏟L⋅U

last_observation.name: Question 8
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Lower Triangular Matrix Given the Elementary Row Operations
last_observation.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+1\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose that a 3×3 matrix H is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear: R2:=R2+R1,R3:=R3−2R1. Given that H has the LU factorization H=LU, then L=

EXPLANATION

Applying R2:=R2+1⋅R1 and then R3:=R3+(−2)⋅R1 is equivalent to multiplying H from the left by the following elementary matrices:

[100010−201]⏟E2⋅[100110001]⏟E1⋅H=U

Now, since E2E1H=U, we can invert E2 and E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E2E1H=UE1H=E2−1UH=E1−1E2−1UH=[100110001]−1[100010−201]−1UH=([100−110001][100010201])UH=[100−110201]⏟L⋅U

Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+1\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-8)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose that a 3×3 matrix H is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear: R2:=R2+2R1,R3:=R3−8R1. Given that H has the LU factorization H=LU, then L=

[1000108−21]

[100−210081]

Submit

EXPLANATION

Applying R2:=R2+2⋅R1 and then R3:=R3+(−8)⋅R1 is equivalent to multiplying H from the left by the following elementary matrices:

[100010−801]⏟E2⋅[100210001]⏟E1⋅H=U

Now, since E2E1H=U, we can invert E2 and E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

last_observation.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-8)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

$$

EXPLANATION
